size.note: Head-and-body length (10.5–16.5 cm) and tail length (1.2–3.8 cm) are given by both Wikipedia and Animal Diversity Web; Wikipedia cites the Animal Diversity Web account for those figures, so they are not independent measurements. Mass of 50–130 g (0.05–0.13 kg) is from Animal Diversity Web only. Those accounts may reflect a historically lumped Cryptomys hottentotus concept; the disagreement with later splits is recorded rather than averaged. The 2016 EWT assessment did not publish measurements. No shoulder height or sexed numerical split was found, although Animal Diversity Web says the breeding pair are the largest animals and that, among the other colony members, males are larger than females.

summary: A short-limbed, cylindrical burrowing rodent, usually grey or brown and sometimes with a white spot on the head. It lives in family colonies underground and feeds on bulbs, corms, tubers and grass rhizomes. The 2011 Kruger checklist uses this name; a later regional assessment assigns Kruger animals to other Cryptomys species.
description: A compact, cylindrical mole-rat with short limbs, thick, evenly coloured fur that is usually grey or brown, and very reduced eyes. Some animals have a white spot on the head. The 2016 regional assessment also records dark sable-brown, light fawny-rufous and smoky-grey animals among captured Cryptomys. Prominent ungrooved, chisel-like incisors are used for digging, feeding and fighting, and long sensory hairs (vibrissae) stand out from the coat over the body and hind legs. Hairy cheeks can close behind the incisors to keep soil out of the throat while the animal digs.
habits: Entirely subterranean and social. Animal Diversity Web and the 2016 EWT assessment describe family colonies of up to 14 animals, often around five, with a single breeding pair — usually the largest female and male — and a workforce of younger “workers” and older “casual workers” that burrow and forage. Wikipedia, citing Animal Diversity Web, treats this arrangement as eusocial. The animals loosen soil with the incisors, pass it back with the feet, and reverse to push batches of earth out of the tunnel. One tunnel system that held 10 adults and 3 young was measured at 1 km. They can live in a wide range of substrates. A Kruger-specific activity study under this name was not found.

diet.summary: A herbivore that feeds mainly on geophytes — plants with underground storage organs — and on grass rhizomes. The 2016 EWT assessment says Cryptomys species specialise on bulbs, corms and tubers, especially those of Albuca, Lachenalia, Ornithogalum, Romulea, Micranthus, Homeria and Oxalis, and also notes that common mole-rats eat some geophytes that contain cardiac glycosides and are toxic to livestock. Animal Diversity Web adds that they consume large amounts of fibre in plant roots. A Kruger-specific diet study under this name was not found.
items: bulbs, corms and tubers, including Albuca, Lachenalia, Ornithogalum, Romulea, Micranthus, Homeria and Oxalis
other underground plant storage organs and roots

young: A seasonal breeder. Wikipedia says mating begins in September and October, and that births are restricted to the southern-hemisphere summer, with one or two litters of up to five pups. Animal Diversity Web gives litters of two to five young, each weighing 8–9 g, and says the pups first leave the nest about five days after birth and begin to eat solids at about 10 days. The 2016 EWT assessment gives litters of two to six young for C. hottentotus and a generation time of roughly three years; that upper litter size is recorded rather than averaged with the figures of five. Gestation is about 81 days, and average age at reproductive maturity is about 450 days. Courtship, as described by Animal Diversity Web and Wikipedia, is started by the male while the female is in oestrus. Kruger-specific birth months were not found.

predators.note: Animal Diversity Web says mole snakes (Pseudaspis cana) prey on mole-rats by entering the tunnel system.
Named by Animal Diversity Web as a predator that may attack mole-rats while they are digging out a burrow or coming to the surface.

Animal Diversity Web says some birds of prey may attack mole-rats while they are digging out a burrow or coming to the surface. The 2016 EWT assessment also states that Cryptomys species are eaten by a wide range of predators, without naming them.

habitat: Lives underground in a wide range of fine- to medium-grained clays and loams, and is often found in human-modified places such as lawns, gardens and golf courses. Animal Diversity Web describes the habitat as the soil of grassy open plains. A Kruger-specific habitat account under this name was not found. The 2016 regional assessment places C. hottentotus, in the narrow sense, in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Free State and Northern Cape, and treats Kruger as part of the range of C. natalensis (clay and loam grassland), with some records in northern Kruger possibly belonging to C. nimrodi.

population.notes: No Kruger census or SANParks count was found. One source reports that, in prime habitats, the density of C. hottentotus can surpass 150 individuals per square kilometre; that figure is not a Kruger count. The 2016 regional assessment gives the population trend of the genus in the assessment region as stable and does not publish a Kruger total. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf.

research.note: This file follows species-list.json in treating the Kruger animal as Cryptomys hottentotus (Common molerat; Afrikaans Vaalmol, as given on the 2011 checklist and on the 2016 EWT assessment, which also lists Grysmol). The 2016 assessment splits the old C. hottentotus into several species that can at present be distinguished only by molecular evidence: it places C. hottentotus, in the narrow sense, in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Free State and Northern Cape, assigns Kruger to C. natalensis, and notes that some records in northern Kruger may belong to C. nimrodi (Matabeleland mole-rat) rather than C. natalensis. Cryptomys and Fukomys cannot be distinguished morphologically. C. natalensis appears in species-list.json as an iNaturalist-only candidate (two research-grade records in place 69020) and is marked there as not included, because it is not on the 2011 SANParks list. This file does not remap the official 2011 name. Wikipedia still gives a broad southern African range for C. hottentotus; Animal Diversity Web limits it to the south-western Cape. Those disagreements are recorded, not averaged. Presence of C. hottentotus in the narrow sense is not supported by the 2016 assessment, so status and monthsPresent are omitted. No Kruger population figure was found. Two licensable photographs of live animals from Western Cape iNaturalist records in place 113055 (southern Africa) were added. The 2016 assessment places narrow-sense C. hottentotus in the Northern Cape, Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Free State, and states that the range of C. natalensis extends into Kruger National Park. This file does not remap the 2011 name. Status and monthsPresent remain omitted.

Two licensable photographs of live animals were added from research-grade iNaturalist observations in place 113055 (southern Africa): an adult on sandy ground at Mossel Bay, Western Cape (CC BY-NC), and an adult at a burrow in the Bitou Local Municipality, Western Cape (CC BY). iNaturalist still had no licensed live-animal photographs in Kruger (place 69020). An earlier South Africa (place 6986) shortlist had only mounds and a container shot.
